# TESSERA: Temporal Embeddings of Surface Spectra for Earth Representation and Analysis

> TESSERA turns a year of satellite observations of every ten-metre square of land into an embedding, which this page calls an annual fingerprint: 128 numbers that describe what the ground is and how it changes through the seasons. The embeddings are made once for the whole planet and published openly, so that a new question needs only a few labels and a small model. It is developed at the University of Cambridge.

This page explains TESSERA as a narrated tour from orbit down to Cambridge, drawn live as a holographic console. It takes the kinds of downstream task in turn on live embeddings (similarity with a 3-D UMAP cloud, a nearest-neighbour classifier and how few labels it needs, and a small U-Net that outlines solar farms as a spatial head), then regression in published studies round the world, and then hands the console to the reader. Eleven narrated side notes explain single ideas in more detail. The notes below give the same facts in plain text.

## How TESSERA works

- Inputs: Sentinel-2's ten optical bands (B2, B3, B4, B5, B6, B7, B8, B8A, B11, B12) and Sentinel-1's radar backscatter in two polarisations (VV and VH), for a whole year.
- The d-pixel: every observation of one pixel over the year, all bands by all dates, with the cloudy or missing dates masked. TESSERA works on each pixel on its own, through time.
- Training: two independent random samples from the same d-pixel are two incomplete views of one place, and the model is trained (with the Barlow Twins objective, mixup and global shuffling) to describe them alike. Version 1 drew 40 observations per view from about 800 million d-pixels. Version 2 draws 8 or 16 per view, trains a 2-billion-weight teacher on about 14 billion d-pixels, and distils it into students of 1 to 44 million weights; at inference it uses every clear observation.
- Nested fingerprints (version 2): the 128 values are ordered so that the first 16, 32 or 64 can be used alone, keeping about 92%, 97% and 99% of the accuracy at an eighth, a quarter and a half of the storage.
- Spatial heads: because the embeddings are per pixel, a small network over a patch of them (such as tze's 41,665-weight solar-farm U-Net) adds the spatial view that finding objects needs.
- The encoder: one transformer branch for Sentinel-2 and one for Sentinel-1, pooled, joined and folded by a small network into 128 numbers, trained to be stored as 8-bit integers with a per-pixel scale. In full precision one year of embeddings for all land would take about a petabyte; as int8 it takes a quarter of that.
- Inference: the frozen encoder makes an annual embedding for every 10 m pixel of land. Pixels with few clear observations are resampled from the ones they have, so the maps have no holes.
- Downstream tasks: a small head (such as a two-layer network, or a nearest-neighbour vote) trained on a few labels. With 1% of the labels, TESSERA scores an F1 of 66.15 on Austrian crop classification, against AlphaEarth's 37.22; on Borneo canopy height its error (12.2 m RMSE) is the lowest of the models tested.

## Paper

- [TESSERA: Temporal Embeddings of Surface Spectra for Earth Representation and Analysis](https://arxiv.org/html/2506.20380): Zhengpeng Feng, Clement Atzberger, Sadiq Jaffer, Jovana Knezevic, Silja Sormunen, Robin Young, Madeline C. Lisaius, Markus Immitzer, Toby Jackson, James Ball, David A. Coomes, Anil Madhavapeddy, Andrew Blake and Srinivasan Keshav. CVPR 2026. [arXiv:2506.20380](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.20380).

- [TESSERA v2: Scaling Pixel-wise Earth Foundation Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.03949): Feng et al., arXiv:2607.03949, 2026. On 14 held-out datasets its 44-million-weight student scores best of the systems compared (0.647, against 0.614 for OlmoEarth-L and TESSERA v1 and 0.590 for AlphaEarth).

## Data

- [TESSERA on Source Cooperative](https://source.coop/tessera/tessera): the embeddings as Zarr v3 stores. This page reads `https://data.source.coop/tessera/tessera/zarr/v1.1-dclimate`: one group per UTM zone (`utm01` to `utm60`) with `embeddings` (int8, time x 128 x y x x, 10 m), `scales` (float32; value = int8 x scale, NaN = no data) and `s2_obs_count`, years 2017 to 2025, and `global_rgb`, a colour pyramid of the 2025 embeddings' first three numbers in EPSG:4326.
- [GeoTessera](https://github.com/ucam-eo/geotessera): a Python library to fetch embeddings for any region.

- [Applications of the TESSERA Geospatial Foundation Model to Diverse Environmental Mapping Tasks](https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.6142416): Feng et al., SSRN 6142416, 2026 (preprint). Crop types in Austria, wildfire burn scars in California, canopy height in Borneo, forest biomass in Finland and tree stocks on agroforestry farms in Brazil.

## Code

- [TESSERA](https://github.com/ucam-eo/tessera): the model, training and inference code and weights.
- [tze](https://github.com/ucam-eo/tze): the TESSERA Zarr Explorer, a map that reads the store in the browser, from which this page's reader and solar-farm model are taken.
- [tessera-eval](https://github.com/ucam-eo/tessera-eval): measures how well a class can be mapped from TESSERA embeddings, with learning curves and spatial hold-outs.

## What the page shows

- The d-pixel is a real field south-west of Cambridge (52.183 N, 0.110 E): its 173 Sentinel-2 passes of 2025 (56 clear), its 198 Sentinel-1 passes, and its real TESSERA embedding.
- The downstream stage reads a 3.2 km window of Cambridge live from the store (100 chunks, about 12 MB), finds everything like Parker's Piece by cosine similarity, and maps farmland, parkland, woodland and town from 14 labels by a nearest-neighbour vote.

## Side notes

- `#/t/sentinels`: **How the Sentinels work.** Sentinel-2 is a pair of satellites orbiting seven hundred and eighty-six kilometres above the Earth. Each one photographs a strip two hundred and ninety kilometres wide, in thirteen bands of light. The sharpest bands show detail down to ten metres. Together, the pair cover the equator every five days. Sentinel-1 carries a radar and orbits six hundred and ninety-three kilometres up. It sends out microwave pulses and measures two kinds of echo. One, called VV, mostly shows the surface of the ground. The other, called VH, mostly shows leaves and branches. Both satellites belong to the European Union's Copernicus programme. Their data are free for anyone to use. Sources: [CVPR paper, Section 3.1](https://arxiv.org/html/2506.20380#S3.SS1).
- `#/t/barlow`: **How Barlow Twins training works.** Barlow Twins is a form of self-supervised learning. That means the model learns from the data itself, without anyone labelling it. Training has two goals. The first goal is consistency. Tessera takes two random samples of clear observations of the same place, from different days of the year. It learns to give both samples nearly the same fingerprint. So a place gets the same fingerprint, whatever the weather was on the days it was seen. The second goal is variety. Each part of the fingerprint should record something different, rather than repeat another part. Tessera checks this across a large batch of places from all over the world. To check the second goal, training uses a much larger version of the fingerprint, which is thrown away when training ends. The researchers found that making this part bigger did not help. The extra effort was better spent on a bigger model and more data. Sources: [CVPR paper, Section 3.3](https://arxiv.org/html/2506.20380#S3.SS3), [TESSERA v2, Section 4](https://arxiv.org/html/2607.03949#S4).
- `#/t/forty`: **How many observations does it use?** Some places are seen clearly only a handful of times a year. Others are seen dozens of times. In training, Tessera sees just eight or sixteen observations of a place at a time, chosen at random. That teaches it to recognise a whole year from a few glimpses. When it makes the fingerprints, it uses every clear observation. Places with a similar number of observations are processed together, so none is thrown away and none is repeated. Sources: [TESSERA v2, Appendix D](https://arxiv.org/html/2607.03949#A4), [CVPR paper, Table 6](https://arxiv.org/html/2506.20380#A1.T6).
- `#/t/storage`: **How the fingerprints are stored.** Each fingerprint is stored as a hundred and twenty-eight whole numbers, from minus a hundred and twenty-seven to a hundred and twenty-seven, plus one scale for the square. Multiplying them together gives the fingerprint back. The model was trained with this rounding in mind, so it loses very little: less than one point of accuracy in the researchers' tests. At full precision, one year of the planet would take a petabyte to store. Stored this way, it takes a quarter of that. The newest fingerprints put their most important values first, so a map that needs to save space can keep just the first sixteen, an eighth of the size, and keep about ninety-two per cent of the accuracy. Sources: [CVPR paper, Section 3.4](https://arxiv.org/html/2506.20380#S3.SS4), [TESSERA v2, Table 28](https://arxiv.org/html/2607.03949#A23.T28).
- `#/t/distil`: **How a large model trains a small one.** Tessera is trained in two steps. First, a large model with two billion weights learns from about fourteen billion d-pixels. It is accurate, but running it over the whole planet for one year would take about a hundred years of work on a single powerful graphics processor. So a much smaller model, with forty-four million weights, is trained to give the same fingerprints. It does the same job with about two years of that work, and scores almost as well. The training also puts the most important information first. The first sixteen values of each fingerprint must rebuild the large model's fingerprint on their own, and so must the first thirty-two and the first sixty-four. Like a set of nesting dolls, each shorter fingerprint sits inside the longer one. Sources: [TESSERA v2, Section 5](https://arxiv.org/html/2607.03949#S5), [Appendix U](https://arxiv.org/html/2607.03949#A21).
- `#/t/cosine`: **How similarity is measured.** Each fingerprint can be drawn as an arrow in a space with a hundred and twenty-eight dimensions. To compare two fingerprints, Tessera's tools measure the angle between their arrows. This is called cosine similarity. Arrows pointing the same way score one. Unrelated arrows score close to zero. On this page, a square counts as similar if its arrow is within about thirty-two degrees of the one you chose. Sources: [tze on GitHub](https://github.com/ucam-eo/tze).
- `#/t/umap`: **How the UMAP cloud is made.** Nobody can picture a hundred and twenty-eight dimensions, so the cloud is a simplified map, made with a method called UMAP. First, UMAP links each square to the fifteen squares with the most similar fingerprints. Then it places all the squares in three dimensions and adjusts them step by step, pulling linked squares together and pushing the others apart. Squares that sit together in the cloud really are similar. The distances between the groups are less reliable. The cloud on this page shows four thousand squares of Cambridge. Sources: [CVPR paper, Figure 16](https://arxiv.org/html/2506.20380#A1.F16).
- `#/t/labels`: **How many labels does a map need?** A program called tessera-eval measures this. Near Vienna, it trains a classifier on more and more labelled pixels of each crop, and tests it each time. Its accuracy climbs quickly at first, then levels off. The test matters too. Pixels next to each other in a field look almost identical, so a test on random pixels flatters the model. A tougher test holds back whole fields that the model has never seen. With a thousand labelled pixels of each crop, the random test scores zero point nine three, and the unseen fields zero point six five. When Tessera was compared with other systems given one per cent, thirty per cent or all of the labels, its lead was widest with one per cent. Sources: [tessera-eval on GitHub](https://github.com/ucam-eo/tessera-eval), [TESSERA v2, Figure 4](https://arxiv.org/html/2607.03949#S5.F4).
- `#/t/unet`: **How the U-Net finds solar farms.** The solar model is a U-Net, a type of neural network shaped like the letter U. The first half shrinks a patch of fingerprints in steps, so the network can see the shape of a whole solar farm. The second half enlarges it back to full size. Links across the U carry the fine detail over, so the edges stay sharp. This network has about forty-one thousand weights, and it runs in your browser. Sources: [tze on GitHub](https://github.com/ucam-eo/tze), [TESSERA v2, Appendix P](https://arxiv.org/html/2607.03949#A16).
- `#/t/heads`: **Which small model goes on top?** The small model on top is called a head. The simplest is a vote among the nearest labelled examples, as in the classifier on this page. Researchers also use random forests, and small neural networks of one to three layers. For a label, the network ends by choosing a class. For a number, it ends with a single output. For shapes, it reads a patch of fingerprints, such as sixty-four by sixty-four squares, with a network such as a U-Net. The choice of head matters. On a set of city mapping tasks, Tessera came a close second with a head that saw one square at a time. With a small head that saw the neighbouring squares as well, it came first. Sources: [Applications paper, Section 2](https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.6142416), [TESSERA v2, Appendix P](https://arxiv.org/html/2607.03949#A16).
- `#/t/compare`: **How Tessera compares with other models.** The researchers compared Tessera with other systems that turn satellite data into fingerprints, including Google DeepMind's AlphaEarth. They tested them on fourteen mapping tasks that played no part in building Tessera, from tree species to road density. Tessera scored best overall, with a model at least seven times smaller than its nearest rivals. Its lead was widest when only one per cent of the labels were used. The newest fingerprints also remove most of the stripes that earlier ones showed along the satellites' paths, and they stay steady from year to year where the land hasn't changed. Sources: [TESSERA v2, Section 5.1](https://arxiv.org/html/2607.03949#S5.SS1), [Figure 9](https://arxiv.org/html/2607.03949#A24.F9).

## Addresses on this site

- `#/s/<stage>`: the story at a stage: orbit, sensors, dpixel, inference, tasks, missions or yours.
- `#/scan/<lat>,<lon>[/<year>]`: the console, scanning live embeddings at a place, for 2025 unless a year from 2017 to 2025 is given.
- `#/t/<note>`: a side note, played from its start.
- `#/script`: the whole script, with the side notes in their places.
- `#/about`: sources and credits.
